strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored setting: discovering 3D keypoints from single images without task-specific 3D annotations or real calibrated multi-view training data. This is a meaningful direction for scalable 3D understanding.

The central idea of converting priors from an image-conditioned multi-view diffusion model into explicit 3D volumetric features is original and technically interesting. Using the diffusion model both for generated-view supervision and as a multi-view feature extractor is a coherent design.

The Human3.6M results provide useful evidence that the method is competitive in a difficult unsupervised single-view setting. It improves over reported single-view unsupervised baselines, e.g. lower MPJPE/N-MPJPE than KeypointNet and Honari et al. under the MLP regressor setting, and it is competitive with some multi-view keypoint discovery methods despite using only a single input image at test time.

The ablations support key design choices: diffusion features substantially improve over a ResNet feature extractor, and increasing the number of virtual views improves performance with saturation around 3-5 views. These experiments directly test the paper's main mechanism.

The qualitative results across in-the-wild humans, dogs, AP-10K animals, GSO objects, and animatable reconstructions suggest the approach may have broader usefulness beyond human pose estimation. The manipulation pipeline is a compelling downstream demonstration.
weaknesses: The empirical support is narrower than the claims. Quantitative evaluation is essentially limited to Human3.6M; the dog, AP-10K, GSO, in-the-wild, and animation results are qualitative. Claims of generalization to arbitrary or diverse categories would be much stronger with quantitative metrics, even if only 2D projection consistency, annotation transfer, or user/structure consistency metrics were available.

The framing of 'without multi-view supervision' is somewhat delicate. The proposed model is trained only from single-view image collections, but it relies heavily on a pretrained multi-view diffusion model whose geometric priors come from external multi-view/3D-related training. This is a reasonable use of foundation-model priors, but the paper should more explicitly distinguish absence of task/dataset multi-view supervision from inherited supervision in the backbone.

The method is not truly a lightweight monocular estimator at inference: it requires foreground masking, running a multi-view diffusion denoising process, extracting intermediate features, and aggregating multiple generated/virtual views. The paper acknowledges cost but does not report runtime, memory, number of denoising steps used at inference, or comparison to feed-forward alternatives.

The evaluation protocol depends on training regressors from discovered keypoints to ground-truth joints. This is standard in unsupervised keypoint discovery, but it can obscure whether the discovered keypoints are semantically stable, anatomically meaningful, or merely predictive after a learned mapping. More direct measures of keypoint consistency, equivariance, and semantic correspondence would strengthen the evidence.

Comparisons are imperfect across methods because baselines use different supervision, numbers of keypoints, regressors, views, and in one case a simplified Human3.6M action subset. The table is useful, but the discussion sometimes overstates conclusions from heterogeneous settings.

Several implementation details are under-specified for reproducibility: the exact SV3D view selection and camera setup, mask generation and failure handling, reconstruction network architecture, feature layers used for aggregation, coordinate normalization/canonical volume bounds, and hyperparameters for MST/skinning are not fully described in the main paper.

The animatable 3D object pipeline is appealing but only demonstrated qualitatively. There is no comparison to rigging, skeleton extraction, or deformation baselines, and no metric for deformation quality, correspondence stability, or user controllability.

The method inherits failure modes from the diffusion model and Grounded SAM preprocessing. For unusual poses, truncation, occlusion, multiple objects, or poor masks, it is unclear whether errors arise from keypoint learning, view synthesis, or preprocessing. A failure analysis would help assess robustness.

strengths: The paper targets an important and difficult setting: monocular 3D keypoint discovery without manual 3D labels or real calibrated multi-view training data. Using an image-conditioned multi-view diffusion model as both a virtual-view generator and a feature source is a timely and potentially useful direction.

The method is conceptually coherent at a high level: diffusion features are aggregated across generated views, unprojected into a 3D volume, converted into heatmaps, and trained through projected edge-map reconstruction. The ablations in Table 2 support two central design choices: diffusion features outperform a ResNet feature substitute, and additional generated views improve performance over the K=1 setting.

The Human3.6M results show some empirical merit. In the single-view unsupervised comparison, the reported 2-layer MLP regressor result improves over KeypointNet and Honari et al. single-view numbers in MPJPE/N-MPJPE, and slightly improves P-MPJPE over Honari et al. single-view.

The qualitative manipulation pipeline is an interesting possible application: estimated keypoints and edge graphs are used to derive a skeleton and skinning weights for diffusion-generated 3D reconstructions.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is much narrower than the claims. Quantitative evaluation is essentially limited to Human3.6M. Generalization to DAVIS, GSO, Stanford Dogs, and AP-10K is presented qualitatively, despite claims about broad in-the-wild and out-of-domain robustness. This makes the strong generalization claims insufficiently supported.

The paper repeatedly frames the method as using only single-view image collections, but the approach relies heavily on a powerful pretrained multi-view diffusion model, foreground masks from Grounded SAM, and known virtual camera parameters chosen for the diffusion model. The source and assumptions of these priors are not adequately accounted for when comparing to prior unsupervised methods.

The evaluation protocol weakens the interpretation of discovered keypoints. Performance is measured by training supervised regressors from predicted keypoints to ground-truth 3D pose on the Human3.6M training split. This assesses whether the representation contains pose information after supervised calibration, not whether the discovered keypoints are semantically stable or directly accurate. The use of nonlinear MLP regressors further obscures what is actually discovered.

Comparisons are not fully convincing. The best multi-view Honari et al. result remains substantially better than the proposed method, while several monocular human-pose baselines use different assumptions and task formulations. The table mixes methods with different numbers of keypoints, regressors, supervision types, and even a simplified six-action subset, making the headline comparison difficult to interpret cleanly.

Important method details are underspecified. The paper does not clearly explain how the feature aggregation network is supervised beyond the downstream reconstruction objective, how the canonical 3D coordinate frame and scale are defined, how Grounded SAM is prompted or used across datasets, how adjacency is regularized to avoid degenerate edge maps, or how failures in generated views affect training labels.

The self-supervised reconstruction objective may admit degenerate or non-semantic solutions, but the paper provides little analysis of keypoint consistency, collapse avoidance, permutation stability, or correspondence across instances. Qualitative figures are not enough to rule out these failure modes.

The animatable-object contribution is only qualitatively demonstrated. There are no quantitative measures of rigging quality, deformation realism, correspondence accuracy, or comparison to automatic rigging/skeleton extraction baselines, so this part reads more like an application demo than a validated contribution.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The method depends on SV3D-p, Grounded SAM, Gaussian Frosting, diffusion timestep/features, generated camera setup, masks, reconstruction architecture, and training details, but many implementation choices are only briefly stated. The claim that code will be released does not compensate for missing details in the manuscript itself.

Clarity is uneven. Several claims are overstated relative to the data, some terminology is imprecise, and there are presentation issues such as typos in figures/tables and ambiguous statements in the implementation section. These are secondary to the evaluation and methodological concerns, but they add to the impression that the paper is not yet mature.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint discovery from only single-view image collections. Leveraging pretrained multi-view diffusion models as both novel-view generators and feature extractors is a compelling idea with clear relevance to scalable 3D understanding.

The method is technically coherent overall: diffusion features are aggregated across generated views, unprojected into a 3D volume using known generated-view cameras, and converted to 3D keypoints through differentiable heatmap regression. The training objective using projected keypoint edge maps and reconstruction is consistent with prior unsupervised keypoint discovery literature.

The quantitative evidence on Human3.6M is reasonably strong for the claimed setting. The method improves over the listed single-view unsupervised baselines, e.g. reaching 119.07 MPJPE / 85.37 P-MPJPE with 32 keypoints and an MLP regressor, and the simplified-subset results are especially competitive.

The ablations are useful and support central design choices: replacing diffusion features with standard features substantially degrades performance, and increasing the number of generated views improves accuracy until saturation around 3-5 views.

The paper demonstrates versatility beyond human pose, including qualitative generalization to DAVIS, GSO, Stanford Dogs, AP-10K species, and an animatable-object pipeline. These results make the contribution feel broader than a narrow benchmark method.

The manuscript is generally clear, well structured, and gives enough implementation detail to understand the main pipeline, including the diffusion backbone, number of views, voxel resolution, optimizer, training length, and losses.
weaknesses: The central claim of learning from only single-view images needs more nuance. The method relies heavily on a pretrained multi-view diffusion model whose own training data and geometric priors may include substantial 3D or multi-view supervision. The paper does not sufficiently discuss this dependency, so the degree to which supervision has merely been transferred from the diffusion backbone remains unclear.

The evaluation beyond Human3.6M is mostly qualitative. Claims about broad in-the-wild, out-of-domain, dog, and cross-species generalization would be more convincing with quantitative metrics, even if indirect, such as 2D projection consistency, correspondence stability, or evaluation against available animal keypoints.

The Human3.6M evaluation depends on a supervised regressor trained from discovered keypoints to ground-truth joints. This is standard in the area, but it limits conclusions about whether the learned keypoints are directly semantic, stable, or useful without labeled calibration. The paper should more clearly separate representation quality from direct 3D pose estimation capability.

Comparisons are somewhat uneven because baselines differ in number of views, number of keypoints, use of object-specific priors, subset choice, and whether they require multi-view data at training or inference. The table is informative, but the acceptance case would be stronger with more carefully matched baselines or reimplemented alternatives under the same generated-view setting.

Some technical details are under-specified for reproducibility: exact SV3D camera choices, diffusion feature layers and aggregation architecture, reconstruction network architecture, foreground mask extraction procedure, prompts/classes for Grounded SAM, and details of the MST edge weighting are not fully described in the main paper.

The formulation of view attention in the unprojection step is mathematically vague: softmax over feature values fk is not clearly defined for vector-valued/keypoint-specific features, making it hard to verify the precise aggregation operation.

The animatable 3D object pipeline is interesting but supported only by qualitative examples. There is no comparison to rigging or deformation baselines and no metric for skeleton quality, skinning quality, or manipulation fidelity, so this part is better viewed as a promising application than a fully validated contribution.

Computational cost is a real limitation: inference requires diffusion denoising to obtain intermediate features and generated views. The paper acknowledges this, but does not report runtime, memory use, or a practical comparison to feed-forward alternatives.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored setting: unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint discovery without requiring calibrated multi-view training images, and the idea of using a pretrained multi-view diffusion model both for virtual-view supervision and intermediate geometric features is timely and technically interesting.

The method is reasonably complete: it combines diffusion feature aggregation, 2D-to-3D unprojection, volumetric keypoint regression, differentiable projected keypoint/edge reconstruction losses, and a downstream object manipulation pipeline.

The Human3.6M quantitative results provide meaningful evidence that the approach can recover useful 3D structure from single images. It improves over the listed single-view unsupervised 3D keypoint baselines in the main comparison, and the ablations support the value of SV3D features, volumetric lifting, and multiple generated viewpoints.

The supplementary ablations are useful, covering number of keypoints, diffusion timestep, amount of training data, affine augmentation, camera perturbation, aggregation strategy, and computational cost. The paper also candidly discusses failure modes such as left-right ambiguity and dependency on diffusion generation quality.
The qualitative results across humans, birds, dogs, and out-of-domain examples suggest the learned representation is visually plausible and potentially useful for downstream 3D manipulation.
weaknesses: The central generality claim is stronger than the evidence. True 3D quantitative evaluation is only shown on Human3.6M; animal and out-of-domain results are mostly qualitative or evaluated only after projecting to 2D. This leaves the core claim of general monocular 3D keypoint discovery across arbitrary categories insufficiently validated.

The preprocessing weakens the claimed unsupervised/no-annotation setting. The supplement states that Human3.6M masks use SAM prompted with provided 2D keypoint locations, and Human3.6M cropping/alignment is based on projected 2D keypoints. This is not merely a presentation detail: it introduces annotation-dependent preprocessing in the main 3D benchmark and should be reflected in the problem statement and comparisons.

The evaluation protocol relies on training regressors from discovered keypoints to ground-truth 3D poses. This is standard in parts of the literature, but it does not fully establish semantic consistency or direct usability of the raw discovered keypoints, especially when increasing the number of keypoints improves errors but may reduce interpretability.

The comparisons are somewhat uneven. On Human3.6M, the method remains well behind the multi-view-trained Honari et al. MLP result, and some baselines use different numbers of keypoints, priors, or supervision assumptions. On CUB, the main table mixes original and reproduced results, and the projected 2D metric does not directly test the proposed 3D contribution.

The animatable 3D object pipeline is appealing but evaluated only qualitatively. There is no quantitative assessment of rig quality, deformation quality, alignment to reconstructed geometry, or comparison to alternative skeleton/rigging methods.

The method is computationally heavy because it depends on SV3D at inference. The supplement reports roughly 11.9 seconds per image and very high FLOPs/VRAM for the diffusion stage, which limits practical usefulness despite the lighter KeyDiff3D module.

Some technical details are under-specified or mathematically unclear. For example, the softmax-based view aggregation over feature vectors is not precisely defined, the learned adjacency/edge supervision may admit degenerate solutions, and reproducibility depends on large external systems such as SV3D, SAM/Grounded-SAM, Gaussian Frosting, and dataset-specific preprocessing choices.

The paper does not sufficiently analyze how much performance comes from the pretrained diffusion model’s category priors or possible exposure to related data, nor does it test robustness under diffusion model failures beyond qualitative examples.

strengths: The paper targets an interesting and timely problem: unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint discovery using priors from multi-view diffusion models. If reliable, this would be useful because it reduces dependence on calibrated multi-view capture and manual 3D annotations.

The central idea of using intermediate SV3D multi-view diffusion features, unprojecting them into a volumetric representation, and predicting 3D heatmaps is technically plausible and reasonably well motivated.

The Human3.6M results show some merit in the narrow evaluated setting: the method improves over single-view unsupervised keypoint baselines and is competitive with some multi-view discovery methods, especially under P-MPJPE after supervised regression.

The ablations are helpful. They support that SV3D features outperform ResNet/CLIP/DINO features in this pipeline, that volumetric 3D prediction is better than 2D prediction plus triangulation, and that virtual viewpoints provide most of the gain.
The paper includes failure cases and reports inference cost, acknowledging left-right ambiguity, dependence on diffusion failures, and the very high computational cost of the diffusion stage.
weaknesses: The main claims are much broader than the evidence. The paper claims unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint estimation across arbitrary object categories, but quantitative 3D evaluation is essentially limited to Human3.6M. For birds and dogs, there is no 3D ground-truth evaluation; the paper only evaluates 2D projections on CUB and provides qualitative examples for dogs and AP-10K.

The animal-category quantitative results are not compelling. On CUB-all, the reported 2D projection error of 7.7 is clearly worse than StableKeypoints at 5.4, and on CUB-aligned the method is only comparable to StableKeypoints and worse than several originally reported 2D baselines. This weakens the claim that the 3D formulation improves general object keypoint discovery.

The evaluation of generalization and animatable 3D objects is almost entirely qualitative. Claims about in-the-wild robustness, out-of-domain transfer to characters and other species, and manipulation usefulness are not supported by metrics, user studies, comparisons, or failure-rate analysis.

The method relies heavily on large pretrained components and external preprocessing: SV3D, Grounded SAM masks, diffusion-generated views and camera parameters, VGG perceptual loss, and Gaussian Frosting for reconstruction. This makes the claimed absence of expensive data acquisition less clean, since much of the geometry prior is inherited from a pretrained multi-view diffusion model whose training data and biases are not analyzed.

The computational burden is severe. The reported diffusion stage requires about 7,787 GFLOPs, 29.5 GB VRAM, and 11.9 seconds per image on an A6000, which is a major practical limitation for a keypoint detector and is not sufficiently balanced by demonstrated downstream gains.

The Human3.6M quantitative protocol depends on fitting a linear or two-layer MLP regressor from discovered keypoints to ground-truth joints. This is a standard proxy in this literature, but it does not by itself prove that the discovered keypoints are semantically meaningful or directly usable without supervision.

The reconstruction objective is not fully convincing as a keypoint discovery signal. In particular, the mask loss compares the rendered soft edge map to a foreground mask, which may encourage coverage or outline-like structures rather than semantically stable articulated keypoints. The paper does not sufficiently analyze this possible shortcut.

The comparison set is uneven. Some baselines use different supervision assumptions, numbers of keypoints, regressors, or datasets/subsets, and the paper emphasizes favorable reproduced CUB results while the originally published 2D baselines often remain stronger. This makes the empirical advantage less clear.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives many implementation details, but reproducing the full method requires several heavyweight pretrained systems, generated multi-view data, mask extraction, and nontrivial preprocessing choices; the sensitivity to these choices is not fully characterized.

Overall, the paper has a worthwhile idea and some promising evidence on Human3.6M, but the broad claims about scalable arbitrary-category 3D keypoint discovery and manipulation are not adequately supported. The balance currently favors rejection rather than acceptance.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and timely problem: unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint discovery for broader object categories, using multi-view diffusion priors to avoid calibrated multi-view capture or 3D labels during the core training objective.

The technical idea is compelling: extracting intermediate SV3D multi-view diffusion features, unprojecting them into a 3D volume, and predicting keypoints from volumetric features is a reasonable and original extension of diffusion features from 2D correspondence/keypoint work to 3D structure discovery.

The experimental evidence on Human3.6M is solid for this problem setting. The method improves over single-view unsupervised baselines and is competitive with some multi-view keypoint discovery methods, while ablations show clear gains from SV3D features, 3D volumetric lifting, and multiple generated views.

The paper is honest about important limitations, including left-right ambiguity and dependence on diffusion failures, and it provides useful additional ablations on number of keypoints, diffusion timestep, training data size, affine augmentation, view misalignment, and computation.

The extension to animatable 3D objects is useful and visually persuasive: aligning discovered keypoints with the diffusion model's coordinate system enables a plausible rigging/manipulation pipeline without manual skeleton design.
weaknesses: The strongest claims about annotation-free training are somewhat weakened by preprocessing dependencies. The appendix states that Human3.6M foreground masks use SAM queried with provided 2D keypoint locations, and cropping/alignment for Human3.6M uses projected 2D keypoints. Even if this is only preprocessing, it conflicts with the headline framing of requiring no manual annotations and should be treated as a material caveat.

Evaluation outside Human3.6M is limited. For CUB, the quantitative evaluation is only 2D projection accuracy, where the method is comparable but not consistently superior to 2D baselines. Stanford Dogs, AP-10K, DAVIS, and GSO results are mostly qualitative, so the broad-category 3D generalization claim is not fully quantitatively supported.

The Human3.6M 3D evaluation relies on training a regressor from discovered keypoints to ground-truth 3D joints, which is standard in this literature but indirect. It does not fully establish that the raw discovered 3D keypoints are semantically stable or immediately usable without a supervised mapping.

The method depends heavily on SV3D quality and cost. The appendix reports very high diffusion-stage inference overhead compared with baselines, and failure cases show that generated-view inconsistency or hallucination directly harms predictions. This limits practical deployment and makes the approach sensitive to the chosen diffusion backbone.

Some methodological details remain underspecified or potentially fragile, such as the exact construction of the canonical 3D coordinate frame aligned to SV3D, the softmax-based view aggregation over feature vectors, and the MST edge weighting formula. These are probably reproducible with code, but the manuscript alone leaves ambiguity.

The animatable-object pipeline is appealing but evaluated mostly qualitatively. There is no quantitative assessment of rig quality, deformation realism, or comparison with alternative automatic rigging/manipulation approaches.
